title: Component Storage & Irradiation: Fridge, Bench, Freezer — Zap the T Cells
summary: Store each blood component at the right temperature, explain what sets red-cell shelf life and why opened or thawed products expire fast, and know why only irradiation prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 41 Hit 3 (only irradiation prevents TA-GVHD; dose; 28-day expiry), Hit 10 (platelet/RBC storage temperatures), Hit 11 (frozen RBCs 10 years; open vs closed deglycerolisation), Hit 16 (CPD/CPDA-1/AS shelf lives), Hit 17 (1–6 °C cold chain, in part), Hit 18 (supernatant K⁺) and Traps 1–2. Checked against Akaraphanth 2026, Adams 2015, Olivo 2015, Elmakki 2023, Sheffield 2016 and Cancelas 2022. Platelet shelf life is taught as 5–7 days (the reviewer says 5; see register flag rv-plt-storage); the reviewer’s end-of-storage pH ≥ 6.0 is not taught (flag rv-plt-ph). Pending: the 1–10 °C transport range and the US 5-day thawed-plasma relabel; HPCs never irradiated; warming thresholds.

objectives: State storage temperatures for red cells, platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate and frozen red cells.
Relate red-cell shelf life to the anticoagulant–preservative and explain storage-related potassium leak.
Explain why opened, thawed or irradiated products have shortened expiry.
Explain why irradiation, not leukoreduction, prevents TA-GVHD, and state the US dose.

scenes.title: Three bags, three mistakes
scenes.altText: Three problem cards appear one by one: a platelet bag found in the refrigerator, a cooler of red cells that arrived at 11 °C, and a leukoreduced unit ordered for a stem-cell transplant patient “so it won’t cause graft-versus-host disease”. A question token asks which rule each one breaks.

cues.text: Three bags reach the issue window. A platelet unit someone put in the fridge overnight.
A cooler of red cells that arrived at eleven degrees. And a leukoreduced unit for a transplant patient — “filtered, so it can’t cause graft-versus-host disease.”
Each one breaks a storage or processing rule. By the end, you’ll know which — and why.

scenes.title: Normal: each component has its own climate
scenes.altText: Three bins labelled Refrigerator 1–6 °C, Room temperature 20–24 °C with agitation, and Freezer. Component tokens slide into place: red cells into the refrigerator; platelets onto the agitator; plasma and cryoprecipitate into the freezer; glycerolised red cells into a deep freezer at −65 °C or colder. Notes explain why: cold slows red-cell metabolism; standard platelets are kept warm because cold-stored platelets are cleared quickly, but warmth lets bacteria grow; freezing preserves labile clotting factors.

cues.text: Every blood component has its own climate. Red cells go in a monitored refrigerator, at one to six degrees, where cold slows their metabolism.

Standard platelets stay at room temperature, twenty to twenty-four degrees, gently agitated. Warm storage keeps them circulating longer after transfusion — but it also lets bacteria grow, so the shelf life is short.
Plasma is frozen to protect the fragile clotting factors, five and eight. Cryoprecipitate is frozen too.
Red cells can even be frozen with glycerol at minus sixty-five or colder — and kept for up to ten years.

scenes.title: What changes: shelf life, leaks and opened bags
scenes.altText: A shelf-life timeline: whole blood or red cells in CPD 21 days, CPDA-1 35 days (adenine added), additive solution 42 days. A potassium bar inside a red-cell bag rises over storage as the sodium–potassium pump slows in the cold, with a warning token for large or neonatal transfusions. Then an opened bag: open-system deglycerolised red cells 24 hours versus closed-system 14 days; thawed plasma loses factor VIII over refrigerated days, so thawed plasma has a short, defined expiry (24 hours as fresh frozen plasma; some systems allow up to 5 days refrigerated).

cues.text: Shelf life depends on what’s in the bag. Red cells in CPD last twenty-one days; CPDA-1 adds adenine for thirty-five; additive solutions reach forty-two.
Storage isn’t harmless. In the cold, the sodium–potassium pump stalls, potassium leaks out, and the supernatant potassium climbs — a risk in massive or neonatal transfusion.
Opening a closed system shortens expiry, because bacteria could get in. Open-system thawed, deglycerolised red cells last twenty-four hours; a closed system allows fourteen days.
Thawing starts a clock too. Factor eight falls day by day in the fridge, so thawed plasma has a short, defined expiry — never indefinite.

scenes.title: In the lab: irradiation stops TA-GVHD — filters don’t
scenes.altText: Donor T-cell tokens in a red-cell bag. In a normal recipient, the recipient’s immune system rejects them. In an immunocompromised recipient, or one who shares an HLA haplotype with the donor, the donor T cells engraft and attack skin, liver, gut and marrow: TA-GVHD, fatal in over 90% of cases. A leukocyte filter removes most white cells but leaves some T cells — not enough protection. The bag passes through an irradiator: T cells are crossed out. Dose card (US FDA): 25 Gy to the centre, at least 15 Gy everywhere; Europe uses 25–40 Gy. Irradiated red cells expire 28 days after irradiation (or at the original expiry if sooner) and leak potassium faster.

cues.text: Every cellular unit carries some living donor T cells. A normal immune system destroys them.

But in a severely immunocompromised patient — or one who shares an HLA type with the donor — those T cells engraft and attack skin, liver, gut and marrow. That’s TA-GVHD, and more than ninety percent of patients die.

Leukoreduction filters out most white cells, but enough T cells slip through. Only irradiation stops them dividing: in the US, twenty-five gray to the center of the bag and at least fifteen everywhere.
Irradiation has a cost. Red cells leak potassium faster, so irradiated red cells expire twenty-eight days after irradiation — or sooner, if the original date comes first.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Leukoreduction prevents TA-GVHD” is crossed out → “Irradiate — filtering leaves enough T cells.” Trap card: “Thawed plasma keeps in the fridge indefinitely” is crossed out → “Factor VIII decays; thawed plasma has a short, defined expiry.” Trap card: “Platelets belong in the fridge like red cells” is crossed out → “Standard platelets: 20–24 °C with agitation; only specially licensed cold-stored platelets are refrigerated.”

cues.text: Trap one: leukoreduction doesn’t prevent TA-GVHD. Irradiation does.
Trap two: thawed plasma can’t sit in the fridge forever. Factor eight decays, so it has a short, defined expiry.
Trap three: standard platelets don’t go in the fridge. They stay at room temperature with agitation — only specially licensed cold-stored platelets are refrigerated.

scenes.title: Fridge, bench, freezer — and zap the T cells
scenes.altText: Memory aid as three kitchen spots: the fridge (red cells, like milk), the bench (platelets, like fresh bread — keeps briefly and can grow mould), and the freezer (plasma and cryo, like ice cream). A fourth token: “Zap the T cells” for irradiation. A card lists where the analogy breaks.

cues.text: Think of a kitchen. Red cells in the fridge, like milk. Platelets on the bench, like fresh bread — good for days, not weeks. Plasma in the freezer. And to stop TA-GVHD: zap the T cells.

Where it breaks: platelets need constant gentle agitation; shelf lives depend on the anticoagulant and on whether the bag was opened; and exact limits follow your regulator — irradiation doses differ between the US and Europe.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Red cells 1–6 °C (21/35/42 d) · platelets 20–24 °C agitated · plasma frozen”, “Only irradiation prevents TA-GVHD · irradiated red cells: 28 d”.

cues.text: Red cells cold, platelets warm and agitated, plasma frozen; opening or thawing starts a short clock; and only irradiation — never a filter — prevents TA-GVHD.

props.label: Red cells 1–6 °C (21/35/42 d) · platelets 20–24 °C agitated · plasma frozen
Only irradiation prevents TA-GVHD · irradiated red cells expire at 28 d

explanation.what: Plain language: each component keeps best in its own climate, every bag has a clock, and only irradiation stops donor lymphocytes from attacking a vulnerable recipient. Scientific terms: red cells 1–6 °C; standard platelets 20–24 °C with continuous agitation (5–7 days); plasma and cryoprecipitate frozen; glycerolised red cells ≤ −65 °C for up to 10 years. CPD 21 d, CPDA-1 35 d, additive solutions 42 d. TA-GVHD is prevented by gamma or X-ray irradiation (US FDA: 25 Gy centre, ≥ 15 Gy anywhere).
explanation.why: Cold slows red-cell glycolysis but stalls the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, so potassium leaks into the supernatant; irradiation adds membrane damage and more leak. Room-temperature platelets circulate longer after transfusion but allow bacterial growth. Labile factors V and VIII decay after thawing. Viable donor T cells can engraft when the recipient cannot reject them (immunodeficiency or HLA haplotype sharing).
explanation.measure: Storage is temperature-monitored; out-of-range units are quarantined and evaluated rather than judged by appearance. Opening a closed system shortens expiry (open-system deglycerolised red cells 24 h vs closed 14 d). Irradiated red cells expire 28 days after irradiation or at the original expiry, whichever comes first.
explanation.differs: Leukoreduction (filters out most leukocytes but leaves some viable T cells) vs irradiation (stops T-cell proliferation; prevents TA-GVHD). Standard room-temperature platelets vs licensed cold-stored platelets (FDA 2023 variance: up to 14 days at 1–6 °C for active bleeding).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: storage temperatures, shelf life by solution, “which prevents TA-GVHD”, irradiated RBC expiry, and thawed-plasma expiry traps.

comparisons.title: Leukoreduction vs irradiation
comparisons.distinguisher: Only irradiation inactivates the T cells that remain.

comparisons.title: Red cells vs platelets
comparisons.distinguisher: Cold for red cells, warm and agitated for platelets.

mnemonic.text: Fridge, bench, freezer — and zap the T cells.
mnemonic.explanation: Red cells in the fridge, platelets on the bench (room temperature), plasma and cryo in the freezer; irradiation (“zap”) prevents TA-GVHD.
mnemonic.limitation: Platelets need continuous agitation; shelf life depends on the solution and whether the bag was opened; exact limits and irradiation doses follow the local regulator.

analogyLimitations: Bins, bags and bars are schematic; bar heights are not measured values.
The kitchen analogy ignores agitation, open vs closed systems and regulator-specific limits.
Pathogen-reduction technologies and the indications list for irradiation are not covered here.
takeaway: Red cells cold, platelets warm and agitated, plasma frozen; opening or thawing starts a short clock; and only irradiation — never a filter — prevents TA-GVHD.

questions.stem: A patient after allogeneic stem-cell transplant needs platelets. The order reads “leukoreduced to prevent TA-GVHD.” What should the blood bank do?

options.text: Provide irradiated platelets; leukoreduction alone does not prevent TA-GVHD
options.rationale: Correct. Filtration leaves enough viable T cells; irradiation stops them proliferating.

options.text: Provide leukoreduced platelets as ordered; filtration removes the T cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. TA-GVHD has occurred despite leukoreduction.
Incorrect. Washing removes plasma proteins, not enough lymphocytes.
Incorrect. CMV status addresses virus transmission, not T-cell engraftment.

questions.stem: A red-cell unit in AS-1 was collected 10 days ago (normal outdate day 42) and irradiated today. What is its new expiry?

options.rationale: Correct. 28 days after irradiation (day 38) comes before the original day-42 outdate.
Incorrect. Irradiated red cells expire 28 days after irradiation when that is sooner.
Incorrect. That applies to open-system processing, not irradiation.
Incorrect. That is a Council of Europe rule for some non-leukoreduced units, not the US rule.

questions.stem: Which storage condition is correct for a standard apheresis platelet unit?

options.rationale: Correct. Standard platelets are stored at room temperature and agitated.
Incorrect. Only specially licensed cold-stored platelets are refrigerated.
Incorrect. Freezing standard platelets destroys them; cryopreserved platelets need DMSO and special processing.
Incorrect. Body temperature is not a storage condition.

claims.text: RBCs 1–6 °C; standard platelets room temperature (20–24 °C) with agitation, 5–7 d, bacterial risk; frozen RBCs ≤ −65 °C up to 10 years.
CPD 21 d, CPDA-1 35 d, additive solutions 42 d.
Stored RBCs leak K⁺ (pump stalls in the cold); irradiation increases the leak; neonatal/massive transfusion hyperkalaemia risk.
Open-system deglycerolised RBCs 24 h; closed system 14 d.
FVIII (and FV) decline in thawed refrigerated plasma; thawed-plasma expiry is short and set by regulation.
TA-GVHD: donor T cells engraft (immunodeficiency, HLA haplotype sharing); > 90% fatal; occurs despite leukoreduction.
US FDA: 25 Gy centre, ≥ 15 Gy anywhere; Council of Europe 25–40 Gy; irradiated RBCs max 28 days (US).
FDA 2023 variance: cold-stored platelets up to 14 days at 1–6 °C for active bleeding.
RBC transport 1–10 °C; US thawed plasma relabelled for up to 5 days at 1–6 °C; HPCs never irradiated.
